query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: By adding a small (approximately 3–5 wt%) amount of a low‐melting, ductile metallic binder phase that is in situ formed during processing, one can create a composite microstructure in the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy that improves its mechanical integrity (reducing crack propagation) without degrading its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: The base (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy exhibits a large caloric effect under applied-field and pressure-field operation but suffers from poor integrity with a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low volume fraction (3–5 wt%) of a ductile, low-melting metallic component (e.g., a compositionally compatible FeCo-based eutectic, rather than In or epoxy) into the alloy melt so that, during solidification, an in situ binder phase forms at grain boundaries and along microcracks.
generation.conditions: Operated under the same applied-field, pressure-field, temperature cycle (around the phase transition temperature), and cyclic mechanical loading conditions as the unmodified alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a well-distributed, ductile binder phase at grain boundaries that bridges microcracks and impedes crack propagation.
generation.mechanism: The ductile binder phase acts to absorb strain energy and blunt crack tips, reinforcing the alloy’s microstructure without interfering with the martensitic (or analogous) phase transformation responsible for the caloric response. Its in situ formation ensures coherent interfaces that preserve transformation kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the pristine alloy, the composite should show a significant improvement in mechanical integrity (target compressive strength increasing toward or above 150 MPa) while maintaining a caloric effect of similar magnitude and reversibility under cyclic applied fields and pressures.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy which exhibits high caloric response but low mechanical strength and a tendency to crack.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under typical operating temperatures near the phase transition, under applied magnetic/pressure fields and cyclic mechanical loading. It assumes that the binder phase remains well dispersed and that its volume fraction is kept below the level where it might dilute the caloric active phase.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how the added binder phase might interact with the intrinsic phase transformation kinetics at a microscopic level, and whether slight compositional changes or interface effects might subtly alter the magnitude or reversibility of the caloric response.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with 3–5 wt% of the selected ductile metallic binder phase added via controlled melting and solidification, and one set of unmodified alloy. Subject both sets to identical applied-field/pressure-field cycling and mechanical loading, while characterizing their caloric response and mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strength and crack propagation behavior).
measurements: Caloric effect magnitude (e.g., entropy or temperature change per cycle)
Compressive strength (MPa) using standard compression tests
Fractography and microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, TEM) to assess binder phase distribution and crack arresting
Cycle-life testing under repeated temperature/field cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the binder-modified samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strength remains similar to or worse than the baseline) OR if there is a measurable degradation in the caloric response compared to the unmodified alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.
